html:
Fixture App turns an iPhone into a tag reader and a tag writer. It runs on the NFC hardware Apple exposes to third-party apps, which means one tag at a time with the Scan sheet open.

What Fixture App does

Hold the top edge of the phone against a tag and the app decodes the NDEF message on it. From there you can edit a record in place or overwrite the tag with a new one. Nothing is uploaded, and no scan history survives closing the app.

The reader understands these payloads:

  • text records, with the language code the tag declares

  • URI records, including tel: and mailto: shortcuts

  • Wi-Fi handover records written by an Android phone

  • vCard payloads, shown as a contact card

Writing is destructive. The app replaces the whole NDEF message rather than appending to it, so whatever was on the tag is gone the moment you tap Write. A locked tag stays readable, and the writer stops with Tag is permanently locked instead of reporting success.

What you need

Supported hardware: iPhone 7 or later, running iOS 16 or later.
Supported tags: ISO 14443 Type A chips formatted for NDEF.

The Chip support matrix lists every chip the reader has been tested against and how much writable memory each one has. An NTAG213 holds 132 bytes, which is a short URL and very little else.

Background scanning

iOS hands a tag to a background app only when the tag carries a URL record matching the app's associated domain. Everything else needs the Scan sheet open in the foreground.

Do not force a tag against the phone

Fixture App needs about two seconds of contact to finish a write. Pressing harder does not shorten that, and a tag creased against a metal case can crack the antenna inside the inlay.

Keep the tag flat and still until the Scan sheet shows the green confirm bar. If the write is interrupted the tag keeps its previous contents, so a failed write is safe to retry.

Where to go next

Start with Scan your first tag, which covers one read and one write on a blank NTAG215. If a tag will not read at all, re-check what you need first. Most failures are a chip the reader cannot address rather than a fault in the tag.
